## Where we left off

- Griffin and Ferreira barely covered morphologically complex words.
- The one place inflection appeared was Property 9, filed next to determiners.
- Levelt Chapter 9 will give us some of the machinery.


::: {.notes}
Last two classes were Griffin and
Ferreira, who said out loud that morphologically complex words were out of
scope. Today is the chapter that has the mechanism.

This is a chapter about sounds, and
we are stealing the architecture out of it. Nobody needs to have followed the
segmental spellout sections.

:::

## Two senses of "morphology"

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Levelt's sense**

The affix *-ed*. Its shape, its syllable, its allomorph.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Our sense**

The feature PAST. Case, number, person, honorification.
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .claim}
It is not the case that Levelt does not discuss "our" morphology. He himself insists on the split: distinguish diacritical features such as
"past", "plural", "third person" **from the affixes they induce**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Levelt's "morphology" is the shape of the affix: how *-ed* is syllabified, which
allomorph surfaces. That is not our course. Our morphology is the feature: PAST,
PLURAL, ACCUSATIVE, honorific.

Read the boxed Levelt sentence out loud, twice if needed. His own architecture
requires the split. Moreover, the reality of morphosyntax is based on the output.

Ask: what other diacritics would you need for a language you know? Take two or
three answers, keep them on the board. Turkish case, Korean honorifics, and
Bulgarian evidentiality all come back on the last slide.
:::

## Some examples:

*I sould be sheeing him soon*


## Some examples:

*I sould be sheeing him soon* [I should be seeing him soon]

::: {.fragment}
The /s/ of *seeing* was taken early. But *seeing* did not come out as *eeing*.
:::

::: {.fragment .claim}
The position and its filler are separate objects.
:::

::: footer
Shattuck-Hufnagel 1979
:::

::: {.notes}
[0:05, 2 min] Read the error aloud, then wait. Let them locate the /s/.

The point is the second half: *seeing* did not lose its /s/. The position was
still there and got filled by the still-available candidate. So the position and
the thing that fills it are separately stored and separately available.

If someone asks how we know the /s/ was "available early," that is exactly the
right question and it is the whole basis for the model. Park it.
:::

## The unit that moved

*I sould be sheeing him soon*

::: {.syl}
::: {.row}
[should]{.wd}[ʃ]{.ons .swap}[ʊd]{.rim}
:::
::: {.row}
[seeing]{.wd}[s]{.ons .swap}[iːɪŋ]{.rim}
:::
:::

- Not two copies of the same /s/ trading places. What exchanged is /ʃ/ and /s/.
- Not *shou* with *see*. The rimes stayed where they were.
- The onset is the slot, and only the onset was refilled.

::: footer
Shattuck-Hufnagel 1979
:::

::: {.notes}
Put the two words on the board split into onset and rime. The exchange is
/ʃ/ with /s/, two different segments, so this is not a case of one /s/ moving
into the place of another.

It is also not the syllable that moved: *shou* and *see* stayed put, only the
onsets traded. The metrical frame holds the slots and the segments are the
fillers.
:::

## Three levels, three kinds of filler {.smaller}

| Level | Frame slots | Fillers |
|---|---|---|
| Morphological / metrical | lemma, number, person, tense | lemmas, **diacritic features** |
| Segmental | stem, affix | morphemes |
| Phonetic | onset, nucleus, coda | segments and clusters |

::: {.notes}
[0:07, 2 min] Do not linger on rows 2 and 3. Point at them, say we are skipping
them, move to row 1.

The line that matters: each level has its own frame with its own slots, and each
slot only accepts one category of filler. That is what makes some errors
possible and others impossible.

Row 1 is our row. Levelt gives it about one paragraph.
:::

## The morphosyntactic address

::: {.frame}
::: {.slot}
[lemma]{.lab}[know]{.fill}
:::
::: {.slot}
[number]{.lab}[any]{.fill}
:::
::: {.slot}
[person]{.lab}[any]{.fill}
:::
::: {.slot}
[tense]{.lab}[past]{.fill}
:::
:::

## The morphosyntactic address

::: {.frame}
::: {.slot}
[lemma]{.lab}[know]{.fill}
:::
::: {.slot}
[number]{.lab}[any]{.fill}
:::
::: {.slot}
[person]{.lab}[any]{.fill}
:::
::: {.slot}
[tense]{.lab}[past]{.fill}
:::
::: {.out}
[unlocks]{.cue} `~`_KNEW_`~`
:::
:::


::: {.frame-note}
Fill every slot and the lock opens. The output is a morpheme string plus a
metrical shape, not sounds.
:::

- One entry *eat*, several items: *eat*, *eats*, *ate*.
- The diacritics select the item.
- Frequent forms are **stored**, not composed. Implication? *arrives* costs no more than *arrive*.

::: footer
Levelt 1989, 9.2.1; Cutler 1983; Stemberger & MacWhinney 1986
:::

::: {.notes}
Walk the frame left to right. Lemma slot, then one slot per
diacritic. Fill all four and the lock opens; what comes out is *knew*.

Stress that the output at this level is a morpheme string plus a metrical shape,
with no sounds yet. The word *knew* on the slide is a label, not a pronunciation.

The stored-not-composed bullet usually gets a reaction. Levelt claims every
frequent inflected form is sitting in the lexicon already. Ask what that leaves for morphology to do. Do not answer;
it is on the last slide.
:::

## `I'd hear one if I knew it`


::: {.frame}
::: {.slot .hit}
[lemma]{.lab}[hear]{.fill}
:::
::: {.slot}
[...]{.lab}[...]{.fill}
:::
::: {.slot .stay}
[tense]{.lab}[present]{.fill}
:::
::: {.out}
[unlocks]{.cue} hear
:::
:::

::: {.frame}
::: {.slot .hit}
[lemma]{.lab}[know]{.fill}
:::
::: {.slot}
[...]{.lab}[...]{.fill}
:::
::: {.slot .stay}
[tense]{.lab}[past]{.fill}
:::
::: {.out}
[unlocks]{.cue} knew
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .claim}
One possible explanation: The lemmas moved between frames and the tense features stayed. *know* landed in the past slot and came out as *knew*, with the irregular form.

Another possibility: "Tense" is dictated by something else, and not lemmas.
:::

::: footer
Garrett 1980
:::

::: {.notes}
[0:12, 3 min] Give them the intended sentence, then the error, then the frames.

The move to make visible: the lemmas swapped between frames and the tense
features stayed in place. *know* arrived in a frame whose tense slot already
said past, so it came out as *knew*. Irregular, and correct.

This is the first piece of evidence that the feature is a separate filler. If
tense travelled with the verb we would have heard *knowed* or *know*.

Good place to check comprehension before moving on.
:::

## `raining on a hitchy day`

Intended: *hitching on a rainy day*.

::: {.fragment}
- Realize: *rain* is a noun, *hitch* is a verb.
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Can we try to write out the process by which this error happens?
- Can it be the same as the hear vs know?
:::

## `raining on a hitchy day`

Intended: *hitching on a rainy day*.

::: {.fragment}
- *rain* is a noun, *hitch* is a verb. Exchanging lemmas are almost always of the same category.
- So this cannot be the same error as *hear* and *knew*.
:::

::: {.fragment .claim}
One level down: stem and root swapped at segmental spellout, where category is
no longer visible.
:::

::: footer
Shattuck-Hufnagel 1979
:::

::: {.notes}
[0:15, 2 min] Quick. The argument is one step.

*rain* is a noun, *hitch* is a verb. Exchanging lemmas are almost always of the same
category, so this cannot be the same kind of error as the last slide.

So it happened one level down, at segmental spellout, where the frame has a stem
slot and an affix slot and no longer knows about syntactic category.
:::

## `they needed to be maded`

::: {.fragment}
1. Level 1 worked. *make* plus PAST unlocked the stem *made*.
2. Level 2 failed. The *-ed* of *needed* was still available and filled the affix slot.
:::

::: {.fragment .claim}
Level 1 delivered the right stem and the affix still went wrong, so PAST and
*-ed* are two different objects.
:::
::: footer
Shattuck-Hufnagel 1979; Fromkin 1971
:::

::: {.notes}
[0:17, 3 min] The best slide in the deck. Build it in two steps.

Step one: level 1 worked perfectly. *make* plus PAST unlocked *made*. The feature
did what it was supposed to.

Step two: level 2 then failed, because the *-ed* of *needed* was still available
and filled the affix slot.

So we get a word that is marked for past twice, by two different mechanisms, at
two different levels. That is the argument that PAST and *-ed* are not the same
object. Nothing else in the chapter makes it this cleanly.

The *churches* aside is optional. Use it only if someone pushes back.
:::

## Where each error happened

| Error | Level | What moved |
|---|---|---|
| *I'd hear one if I knew it* | morphological | lemma, diacritic stayed |
| *raining on a hitchy day* | segmental | stem and root |
| *they needed to be maded* | segmental | affix only |

::: {.fragment .claim}
Surface similarity is no guide to which address failed.
:::

::: {.notes}
[0:20, 1 min. CUT THIS IF YOU ARE BEHIND.] Just a recap table. Point at the three
rows, say the line about surface similarity, move on.
:::

##

What do we care about? Morphosyntax or diacritics.

Q: Is there a diacritic exchange or substitution?

::: {.prompt}
- What would an exchange of two diacritic features look like?
- Two *features* swapping while the words stay in place.
:::

::: {.notes}
[0:26, 2 min] Pose it and let it sit. Every other row on the ladder has attested
exchanges.

Be precise about what we are asking for: not two words swapping, but two
features swapping while the words stay in place. Something like intending "the
cats were sleeping" and producing "the cat were sleeping" with the plural having
gone somewhere else.

Take guesses. Do not resolve it yet.
:::

## One candidate (questionable)

*The key to the cabinets **are** rusty.*

::: {.fragment}
Wrong filler, right slot: PLURAL from *cabinets* got into the number slot of the
verb's address.
:::

::: {.fragment .claim}
That is a diacritic **substitution**, not an exchange. The displaced singular
does not appear anywhere else.
:::

::: {.fragment .prompt}
- Think about agreement again: how does a feature get from *cabinets* to a verb
  that far away?
- Are there phonological errors that depend on something equally far away? Vowel
  harmony?
:::


::: footer
Bock & Miller 1991
:::

::: {.notes}
[0:28, 3 min] Give them the sentence and let someone notice it sounds fine.

That is the point. Agreement attraction is a wrong filler in the right slot:
PLURAL came from *cabinets* and landed in the number slot of the verb's address.
Structurally that is a diacritic error.

Then the catch: it is a substitution, not an exchange. Nobody produces the
displaced singular somewhere else in the sentence.

Discussion beat, 1 minute: is that a fact about features, or about how we count
errors? An exchange needs both halves to surface. If a feature has no audible
home of its own, you would never see the second half.

Then the long-distance question. Nothing in the frame says how far a filler can
travel. Ask whether phonology does anything comparable: vowel harmony crosses a
whole word, so a harmony error would be the phonological analogue.
:::



## One more experiment

- Okay, there was one cool experiment in the chapter that I want you to think
  about.

## Treiman's game

First you learn the items by repeating them, what is the rule you infer?

::: {.game}
::: {.pair}
[kig]{.src} → kaz ig
:::
::: {.pair}
[buf]{.src} → baz uf
:::
::: {.pair}
[tep]{.src} → taz ep
:::
::: {.pair}
[nol]{.src} → naz ol
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
Take the onset, add *az*, then say the rime.
:::

::: footer
Treiman 1983, 1984
:::

::: {.notes}
[0:33, 2 min] Play it. Read the four training pairs out loud and have them repeat.
Do not explain the rule; let them infer it.

Then ask someone to state the rule. Take the onset, add *az*, say the rime.

Point out what just happened: they now have a productive rule over a unit nobody
named for them.
:::

## `skef`

Two answers fit the training data.

::: {.split}
::: {.win}
skaz ef
[onset cluster held]{.verdict}
:::
::: {.win}
saz kef
[cluster broken]{.verdict}
:::
:::

## `skef`

Two answers fit the training data.

::: {.split}
::: {.win}
skaz ef
[onset cluster held]{.verdict}
:::
::: {.lose}
saz kef
[cluster broken]{.verdict}
:::
:::

::: {.claim}
Almost all responses were the first. The onset cluster moves as a unit.
:::


::: {.notes}
[0:35, 2 min] Ask for the answer before you advance. Somebody will say *skaz ef*.
Ask if anyone said *saz kef*. Usually nobody does.

Both answers fit the training data exactly. The training set had no clusters in
it, so the game does not tell you what to do with /sk/. They chose anyway, and
they all chose the same way.

That is evidence that the onset cluster is one addressable unit.
:::

## In-class exercise

::: {.prompt}
Design one of these, then tell us what it predicts.
:::

1. Run Treiman's game with L2 speakers whose first language does not allow /sk/
   onsets. What do you expect them to answer for *skef*, and what would either
   answer tell you?
2. Build a game whose rule is over a morphosyntactic slot instead of a syllable
   constituent. What is the frame, what is the slot, what is the filler?

::: {.notes}
[DISCUSSION. This is the point of the class.] Hand it over and get out of the
way. One I like: have English speakers learn either something they have the
'morphological' slot for or something they don't. Maybe honorific agreement?
Evidentiality? Or maybe the possessive-genitive.

For the L2 version: if Japanese or Turkish speakers answer *saz kef*, is that
their L1 grammar showing, or did they just learn the game differently? The
question to land is what evidence would tell you they have an /sk/ slot rather
than a memorized /sk/ string. Somebody usually proposes a novel cluster.

For the morphosyntactic version, the hard part is the analogue of "a wrong
answer that was still legal." In the syllable game both answers were consistent
with training. What is the morphosyntactic version of that fork? Turkish
accusative, Korean *-si-*, whatever they know.

Warning to give them if there is time: distinctive features are real units and
they do not move in speech errors. Fromkin's classic feature slips (*clear plus
sky*, *mity the due teacher*) are almost the only ones anyone has.
Multiple-feature shifts are far too frequent to be coincidences of
single-feature ones. So if
diacritic features behave like distinctive features, a null result in the game
is uninterpretable: an absent unit and an immovable unit give you the same data.
Design against that. (Fromkin 1971; Shattuck-Hufnagel & Klatt 1979.)

If it goes well this becomes somebody's final project. Say so.
:::


## Takeaways

1. A frame is an address. Fill every slot and a stored form is unlocked.
2. Level 1 fillers are lemmas plus diacritic features. That is the morphosyntax.
3. PAST and *-ed* fail independently: *knew* proves one, *maded* proves the other.
4. Only units with slots can slip, which excludes syllables and features.
5. The diacritic row of the ladder is still empty. Whether it can be filled is an
   open question, and a testable one.

::: {.notes}
[0:48, 1 min] Read 2 and 3 aloud, then stop on 5 and say it is the one you want
them thinking about. Skip the rest, they can read.
:::

# Extra slides {.divider}

## The word sketch

TOT states: you have the metrical shape and the first sound, not the word.

- First phoneme correct 60 to 70 percent of the time.
- Syllable count correct 60 to 80 percent, plus which one is stressed.
- A **phonological** blocker induces TOT. A semantic one does not.

::: {.fragment .claim}
Form comes out in layers, and the layers can come apart.
:::

::: footer
Brown & McNeill 1966; Jones & Langford 1987
:::

::: {.notes}
[APPENDIX] Use only if someone asks how we know form comes in layers, or if you
have five minutes spare after the Treiman discussion. TOT gives you the metrical
shape and the onset with no segments, and a phonological blocker induces it while
a semantic one does not.
:::

## The Unit-Similarity Constraint

::: {.claim}
The intruder is of the same level and the same category as the target.
:::

- Lemmas with lemmas, stems with stems, affixes with affixes, onsets with onsets.
- Stems never exchange with affixes.
- Affixes never exchange with onsets.

::: footer
Shattuck-Hufnagel 1979
:::

::: {.notes}
[APPENDIX] The formal statement of what the ladder shows. Pull it up if the class
wants the principle named rather than demonstrated. Shattuck-Hufnagel 1979.
:::
